emerging_technology: Large Language Models (LLMs) as deployable general-purpose generative AI systems supporting multiple forms of cognitive or knowledge work
intended_application: LLM-assisted software development: code generation, explanation, testing assistance, debugging support and technical documentation
business_need: Improve the same software-development functions under limited resources and rapid experimentation
users_stakeholders: Developers, engineering managers, security reviewers, customers and data owners
capabilities_constraints: Hypothetical assumptions: AI familiarity, limited engineering resources, short financial runway and rapid experimentation; security, code quality and operational dependence remain constraints; no local benefit metrics supplied
risk_consequence_context: Insecure or defective code, confidentiality loss, limited review capacity, vendor dependence and runway pressure
management_question: Whether faster and broader integration of the same LLM-assisted development functions is justified
time_horizon: Hypothetical decision horizon: next 6 months, including a bounded pilot and review; not an observed organizational plan
additional_context:
EVIDENCE SNAPSHOT v0.2 — original-source review on 25 October 2026 (America/New_York).
This is a bounded research dossier for actual testing, NOT an agent response or predetermined classification. Source claims were checked in originals, not independently replicated. No assumption that older experiments measure current tools. Seven sources selected for support and opposition; this is not a systematic or exhaustive current review. All four cases use this identical block.

COURSE METHOD: C11 = Andres Fortino, Chapter 11: Identifying Promethean Technologies, August 2026 draft rev 0.1, supplied PDF. §§11.2 (pp. 3–4) and 11.7 (pp. 9–10): usable system, precise barrier statement, suppression test, cross-tier dissolution and six criteria only after gates. Roughly tenfold improvement needs a valid baseline. §11.5: author's working framework, not established academic consensus. Pages 10–11 provisionally classify generative AI as Potential Promethean with irreversibility unverified. Acknowledge and evaluate this calibration, not as empirical proof that each LLM system clears all gates. Assignment 4/common course documents require three levels, opposing evidence, hype resistance and qualification/abstention. All course documents were inspected.

S1 — Sida Peng, Eirini Kalliamvakou, Peter Cihon, Mert Demirer, The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot, 13 February 2023, arXiv v1; https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590v1 (full PDF inspected, Study Design/Results pp. 3–5; limitations pp. 7–8). Randomized 95 professional programmers on a standardized JavaScript HTTP-server task in May–June 2022. Among completers (35 per group), mean time was 71.17 versus 160.89 minutes: 55.8% less time. Analyst arithmetic: 160.89/71.17 ~= 2.26x task-time ratio, NOT 10x or 55.8% more throughput. Completion used 12 tests; paper explicitly did not study code-quality effects. Narrow task, older tool, conditional-completer estimate; Microsoft/GitHub affiliations. Supports code-assistance capability, not universal speedup, autonomous correctness or categorical dissolution.

S2 — Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond, Generative AI at Work, NBER Working Paper 31161, April 2023 revised November 2023; https://www.nber.org/papers/w31161 and https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w31161/w31161.pdf (abstract PDF p. 2, data p. 13, empirical strategy p. 15, conclusion PDF pp. 29–30 inspected). Staggered rollout to customer-support workers; 5,179 agents, difference-in-differences, not a randomized trial. Reports 14% higher issues resolved/hour (~1.14x), larger gains for novices/lower-skilled workers and little effect among the most experienced/high-skilled. Supports usefulness beyond code and possible expertise diffusion; does not prove 10x gains, human replacement, universal access or long-run societal effects. Working-paper version verified; do not silently substitute estimates from the 2025 journal version merely linked by NBER. One setting, identifying assumptions and generalizability limits apply.

S3 — Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR), Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, issuer report 10 July 2025 / retrieved arXiv v2 25 July 2025; https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089v2 and https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/ (paper abstract, design/results and original issuer report inspected). 16 experienced contributors, 246 tasks in familiar mature repositories, randomized AI access, early-2025 tools primarily Cursor/Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet. AI allowed increased task time by 19%. Developers nevertheless perceived gains. Specific historical setting, not proof all/current developers are slowed. The issuer now explicitly warns these historical results are out of date: read S4 and S5 with S3.

S4 — Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud (METR), We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design, 24 February 2026; https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/ (original summary, selection analysis and design details inspected). Follow-up on later-2025 tools: issuer calls its current productivity signal unreliable because developers/tasks selected out of no-AI conditions, changed pay, quality differences and concurrent agents complicating time reports. Authors believe speedup likely increased but say data gives very weak evidence for magnitude. This qualifies the older negative result and supports investigating changed workflows; it is NOT reliable proof of a precise current gain. Reluctance to do tasks without AI is not a demonstrated societal suppression-test failure.

S5 — Joel Becker (METR), Measuring the Self-Reported Impact of Early-2026 AI on Technical Worker Productivity, 11 May 2026; https://metr.org/blog/2026-05-11-ai-usage-survey/ (summary/methodology/results/qualitative cautions inspected). Survey February–April 2026 of 349 technical workers: medians across value measures 1.4–2x; median perceived speed 3x. These are SELF-REPORTED counterfactuals, NOT measured causal multipliers. Convenience sampling, low response, possible inflated high estimates and distinction between speed and value are explicit. Current perceived-usefulness signal, not verified 10x or irreversible dependence. S3–S5 share an issuer and are not independent replications.

S6 — Tao Tu, Anil Palepu, Mike Schaekermann et al. (Google Research/Google DeepMind), Towards Conversational Diagnostic AI, 11 January 2024, arXiv v1; https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.05654v1 (original PDF abstract, study design/results and Discussion pp. 17–20 inspected). Specialized LLM-based AMIE compared with 20 primary-care physicians across 149 simulated scenarios in randomized double-blind crossover text consultations with patient actors. Authors report better diagnostic accuracy and many rated axes in that evaluation. Simulation, specialized system and text interface unfamiliar to clinicians limit generalization; real clinical safety, routine documentation benefit and generic LLM performance are NOT established. No patient-outcome or regulatory approval claim is supported. Supports further capability investigation, not clinical deployment authorization.

S7 — Neil Perry, Megha Srivastava, Deepak Kumar, Dan Boneh, Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?, initial preprint 7 November 2022, CCS 2023, retrieved arXiv v3 18 December 2023; https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03622v3 (abstract, study design/Table 1 and security results inspected; DOI 10.1145/3576915.3623157). 47 participants, five analyzed security-related tasks, assistant based on codex-davinci-002. Authors find generally less secure code with assistance and greater perceived security; insecure solutions more often in four of five tasks. Small mostly-student sample, old model and task heterogeneity; not a current universal vulnerability rate. Supports separate security/oversight evaluation and opposes equating generation with reliable delivery; does not negate all capability gains.

EVIDENCE BOUNDARIES / ANTI-HYPE: funding, media, valuations, popularity, novelty, aggressive posture and organizational enthusiasm are not independent evidence of categorical dissolution. Positive task studies and contrary security/productivity findings concern different populations, tasks, tools and dates; do not average them into one universal effect or treat differences as identical-task replications. No measured broad 10x quality-adjusted performance, cost or access change is established by this dossier. Cost/access evidence is incomplete. Code/support/simulated medicine demonstrate or explore multiple domains, not automatically multiple civilizational tiers. Paradigm change and catalytic effects remain interpretations/hypotheses unless further supported. Novice benefits suggest expertise diffusion but do not establish universal democratization. No societal removal experiment or mature long-run irreversible dependence has been verified; perceived dependence is not enough. Distinguish component, specialized system and the general-purpose system under review. Follow the barrier gates before six-criterion scoring; qualify or abstain where needed.

UNVERIFIED / LOCAL GAPS: attempted NIST AI 600-1, WHO guidance and a JAMA page returned 403; no contents or claims from those are admitted. No original clinical-documentation effectiveness trial or jurisdiction-specific regulatory analysis is supplied. No local cost/benefit, security incident, safety validation or actual organization outcome exists for these hypothetical cases. Clinical documentation and decision support need separate assessments; request missing evidence rather than infer readiness. General significance, application consequences and organization-specific action must remain separate. A qualified/unresolved or lower classification is acceptable, as is a defensible Potential Promethean assessment; no label is predetermined. Explain missing evidence and observations that would change each gate/criterion and the bounded recommendation.
END SHARED EVIDENCE SNAPSHOT v0.2

All organization descriptions and the six-month horizon are hypothetical test assumptions, not verified deployments or plans.
